ctx: Jude is a one-chapter letter from the brother of James, written in haste. His reason is plain:

ctx.q: contend earnestly for the faith having been delivered once for all to the saints

ctx: . Verses 5 to 19 are his evidence: a people saved from Egypt and later destroyed, angels who left their place, Sodom, Cain, Balaam, Korah. Enoch is the last witness he calls.

, where he walks with God and is taken. The book of 1 Enoch is attributed to him and survives complete in Ge'ez, in the Ethiopian Orthodox Church. The English text of 1 Enoch in this archive is R. H. Charles' translation.

inv.q: And Enoch, the seventh from Adam, also prophesied as to these, saying

inv: . He does not write 'as some say' or 'as the story goes'. He says Enoch prophesied, and then he quotes. Jude is calling a witness, as the law of witness requires, to stand beside the Scriptures his readers already held.
Now lay the two texts side by side. Jude:

inv.q: Behold, the Lord came amidst myriads of His holy ones
to do judgment against all, and to convict all the ungodly
He cometh with ten thousands of His holy ones
To execute judgement upon all, And to destroy all the ungodly: And to convict all flesh

inv: . The coming with holy ones, the judgment on all, the conviction of the ungodly for their works and for the hard things sinners have spoken against Him: all of it is in both. One is Greek rendered into English and the other is Ge'ez rendered into English, so we should not expect identical words. We should expect the same content, and we find it.

What this shows, and what it does not. It shows that an apostle's letter, which every Bible includes, treats words found in 1 Enoch as prophecy and uses them as evidence in an argument about judgment. It does not, by itself, settle whether Jude meant to certify the whole book. That is the canon question, and Kingdom Code's essays take it up at length. The investigation starts with what is in front of us: Jude had Enoch's words, and he called them prophecy.
Enoch says what his testimony was for:

inv.q: not for this generation, but for a remote one which is for to come

inv: . A witness addressed to a later generation is a witness that has to be kept until it is needed. Study 7 returns to what it takes to keep it.

take: Jude introduces words found in 1 Enoch with the word 'prophesied'. Whatever one concludes about the whole book, the New Testament itself puts this testimony on the table.
